title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), Mental Models: The Best Way to Make Intelligent Decisions
text:
## What a mental model is

A mental model is a simplified explanation of how something works. Models compress complexity into manageable conceptual chunks, highlighting the key information while filtering out irrelevant detail. No single model captures the full richness of reality, so a thinker needs many, drawn from many disciplines.

## The latticework of mental models

Charlie Munger frames the foundational principle: if you want to be a good thinker, you must develop a mind that can jump the jurisdictional boundaries. You do not have to know it all. The goal is to draw the best big ideas from all the disciplines rather than mastering everything. Held together, these ideas form a latticework: interconnected models from multiple domains that reinforce and illuminate one another. When a new fact or experience arrives, you hang it on the latticework you already have.

## The core general thinking tools

Seven general-purpose models apply across almost any situation:

1. The Map is Not the Territory. Mental representations differ fundamentally from reality itself. A map is a reduction of what it represents, and you must choose your mapmakers wisely and remember the map can be wrong or out of date.

2. Circle of Competence. Know the boundary between what you understand reliably and where you lack expertise. Operating inside your circle produces effectiveness; knowing its edge is as important as knowing its contents.

3. First Principles Thinking. Break a problem into its fundamental truths, stripping away layers of assumption, then reason up from there.

4. Second-Order Thinking. Play the long game by anticipating ripple effects. Ask And then what? to see the consequences of the consequences.

5. Probabilistic Thinking. Navigate uncertainty by identifying what matters and calculating the odds, updating constantly as new information arrives.

6. Inversion. Flip the problem. Instead of How do I succeed? ask What guarantees failure? and then avoid those things.

7. Occam's Razor. When competing explanations exist, the correct explanation is most likely the simplest one, the one with the fewest assumptions.

## The disciplines the latticework spans

The most useful models come from physics, chemistry and biology, systems thinking, mathematics and numeracy, economics and microeconomics, military strategy, human nature and the cognitive biases, and art and aesthetics. Reading widely across these domains is how you acquire the models. The payoff is better decisions because you can apply insight from one field to a problem in another.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), First Principles: The Building Blocks of True Knowledge
text:
## What first-principles thinking is

First-principles thinking breaks a complex problem down by separating what we know is absolutely true from anything that is an assumption. If you know the first principles of something, you can build the rest of your knowledge around them to produce something new. Plato, Aristotle and Descartes all sought foundational knowledge that could serve as a constant base for broader systems. Modern application does not require capital-T absolute truth; it requires finding the irreducible elements within a specific context. First principles do not provide a checklist of things that will always be true; our understanding evolves as we gain more knowledge.

## Two techniques for getting to first principles

Socratic questioning is a disciplined six-step process: clarify your thinking and the origin of your ideas; challenge your assumptions; seek the evidence that supports them; consider alternative perspectives; examine the consequences and implications; and then question the original question itself.

The Five Whys is the childhood instinct of asking Why? repeatedly, drilling down through layers of cause until you reach a foundational truth rather than an assumption or an opinion.

## First principles versus reasoning by analogy

Reasoning by analogy is doing this because it is like something else, copying what others do with small variations. First-principles reasoning requires boiling things down to the most fundamental truths and reasoning up from there. Elon Musk notes it takes a lot more mental energy to reason from first principles than by analogy, which is why most people default to analogy.

## Concrete examples

Battery costs: the industry assumed battery packs cost about 600 dollars per kilowatt-hour and always would. Broken into raw materials, cobalt, nickel, aluminum, carbon, polymers and steel, the commodity market value was about 80 dollars per kilowatt-hour. The fixed cost was an assumption, not a law, so dramatic reduction was possible.

Rockets: the raw material cost of a rocket is roughly 2 percent of the typical launch price. If materials are that cheap, the expense comes from outdated mindsets and processes, not from physics.

CD Baby: Derek Sivers reduced the business to a single first principle, happy customers, and built to that, reaching roughly 4 million dollars a month in revenue while avoiding unnecessary overhead.

## Limiting beliefs first principles dissolve

Common assumptions collapse under first-principles scrutiny: I don't have a good memory; there is too much information (focus instead on the 3 to 5 critical variables that affect the outcome); all the good ideas are taken; we must move first (the iPhone and Microsoft won as improvers, not pioneers); it has never been done before (irrelevant, assess what is physically possible). In a world focused on incremental improvement, first-principles thinking is a competitive advantage precisely because it is not widely practiced.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), Inversion and the Power of Avoiding Stupidity
text:
## Origin of inversion

Inversion traces to the German mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi, whose maxim was man muss immer umkehren, loosely, invert, always invert. As Charlie Munger explains, Jacobi knew that it is in the nature of things that many hard problems are best solved when they are addressed backward. Rather than starting from the goal and working forward, you start from the outcome you want to avoid and work back.

## Munger's application

Munger, Warren Buffett's business partner, popularized inversion with characteristic wit: All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there. The point is to think hard about what you want to avoid, then simply steer clear of it.

## Two approaches to a problem

There is additive, forward thinking, which focuses on the actions that foster a desired outcome, and there is subtractive, inversion thinking, which asks what would guarantee the opposite of what you want, then removes those things. To spark innovation, do not only list practices that encourage it; identify everything that discourages innovation and eliminate those behaviors. To build a good life, consider what prescriptions would ensure misery, and avoid them.

## The central insight

Avoiding stupidity is easier than seeking brilliance. Inversion acts as an avoiding-stupidity filter. It is unglamorous, but it is accessible and reliable: it is often easier to identify and remove the obstacles to success than to engineer success directly.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), Second-Order Thinking: What Smart People Use to Outperform
text:
## Definition

Second-order thinking examines the long-term and downstream consequences of a decision by pushing the mind past the immediate problem. It is the practice of thinking things all the way through to understand the cascading effects across time and across a system.

## Howard Marks' two levels

In The Most Important Thing, Howard Marks distinguishes two levels of thought. First-level thinking is simplistic and superficial: it requires only an opinion about the immediate outcome, for example a favorable outlook means the stock rises. Second-level thinking is deep, complex and convoluted: it examines interactions, the reactions of others, and consequences over time. Because first-level thinking is common, the second-level thinker gains an edge precisely where others stop.

## First-order versus second-order consequences

First-order thinking is fast and intuitive; it solves the immediate problem without weighing the ripple effects. The chocolate bar example: eating it solves hunger now but ignores what repeated consumption does to health. Second-order thinking is deliberate. It asks And then what? again and again, and it maps consequences across different timeframes, for instance 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years, while accounting for how employees, competitors, suppliers and regulators will respond.

## Why it creates an advantage

Many of the highest-value moves are first-order negative, second-order positive: they look unattractive in the short run but produce strong long-term results. People stuck at first-order thinking never see these opportunities, so the second-order thinker can act where others will not.

## Practical methods

Habitually ask And then what? Map consequences across extended timeframes. Keep a template that documents first-, second-, and third-order effects. Systematically consider how each stakeholder will react to your decision.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), Understanding Your Circle of Competence
text:
## What the circle of competence is

A circle of competence is an area where you hold substantial, earned knowledge and a genuine advantage over others. Its size matters far less than knowing precisely where its boundary lies.

## The perimeter principle

Inside your circle you operate with an edge. As you approach the perimeter, the limit of your knowledge, that advantage shrinks; cross it and your edge transfers to the people who understand the terrain better. Munger frames the aim plainly: I look for a game where I am wise and they are stupid. The real danger outside the circle is what remains invisible to you: confidence usually declines slower than actual competence, which creates dangerous blind spots.

## Buffett's illustration

Warren Buffett points to Rose Blumkin, who built Nebraska's largest furniture store by restricting herself to furniture and real estate, the domains she truly understood. She would not diversify into stocks because, in Buffett's words, She understands cash. She understands furniture. Her narrow focus was her greatest strength.

## Three practices

First, honest self-assessment: separate what you genuinely know from what you only assume you know. Munger warns it is better to have an IQ of 160 and think it is 150 than an IQ of 160 and think it is 200. Second, prioritize outcome over ego when deciding whether to act inside or outside your domain. Third, expand the circle selectively and slowly through disciplined work, while keeping realistic boundaries.

## The permission to say no

Berkshire Hathaway avoided pharmaceuticals entirely because, as Buffett put it, we have got no edge in predicting which drugs will succeed. Saying no was not weakness; it freed resources for stronger opportunities squarely inside the circle.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), Occam's Razor: The Simplest Solution Is Usually Correct
text:
## The principle

Occam's razor holds that among competing hypotheses, the one with the fewest assumptions should be selected: the simplest explanation is preferable to one that is more complex. The historical formulation is that entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity, a lineage running through Aristotle and Robert Grosseteste.

## The critical caution

Simplicity alone is not proof. A conclusion cannot rely just on its simplicity; it must be backed by empirical evidence. The simpler explanation, although it has a higher chance of being correct, is not always true. We should never blindly follow the result of applying a mental model when logic, experience, or empirical evidence contradicts it.

## Concrete examples

Einstein's formulation captures the balance: everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler. In medicine, the training maxim is when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras, prioritizing common diagnoses over rare ones. In law, Jeremy Bentham held that punishments should not cause more pain than they prevent, favoring the least elaborate remedy that still works. The razor is a tie-breaker and a starting point for investigation, not a substitute for evidence.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), The Wisdom of Hanlon's Razor
text:
## The principle

Hanlon's razor states: never attribute to malice that which can be adequately explained by neglect. Napoleon expressed the same idea: never ascribe to malice that which is adequately explained by incompetence. It is a default assumption, not a certainty: when something goes wrong, first reach for the mundane explanation before the sinister one.

## The reasoning

The razor rests on a simple observation: incompetence far outweighs malevolence in explaining human behavior. People make mistakes, forget things, speak without thinking and act on incomplete information. These failures often look intentional from the outside but are far more mundane in origin.

## Why it matters for decision-making

Assuming neglect rather than malice transforms your response. Instead of becoming defensive or retaliatory, you approach the situation with empathy and clarity. This reduces emotional reactivity and frees you to solve the actual problem rather than fight an imagined enemy.

## Concrete examples

When Apple's Siri could not return abortion clinic searches, many assumed misogyny; it was a programming oversight. A tourist struggling with the local language is not deliberately wasting your time; they simply lack fluency. A string of taxi mistakes by different drivers feels malicious because the memories are vivid, yet each is a simple error.

## The caveat

The razor is a default, not a blindfold. When genuine malice is actually confirmed, the appropriate response shifts, and you should act decisively rather than keep excusing bad actors.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), The Map Is Not the Territory
text:
## The principle

The map of reality is not reality itself. Maps are reductions of what they represent; if a map were perfectly accurate it would cease to be a useful simplification. A map is also a snapshot from a point in time, and it may represent something that no longer exists. The idea traces to Alfred Korzybski, who argued that we experience the world through abstractions, never the thing itself.

## Why maps are necessary and limited

Maps reduce complexity so we can act: financial statements condense thousands of transactions, policy documents compress procedure, performance reviews summarize a year of work. Their usefulness comes from leaving things out. That same reduction is their danger, because the omitted detail can be exactly what matters.

## The danger of mistaking the map for the territory

When we mistake the map for the territory, we start to think we have all the answers, and we build static rules disconnected from a dynamic world. Jeff Bezos found that Amazon's wait-time data showed under sixty seconds while customers reported waits that felt much longer. His conclusion: when the data and the anecdotes disagree, the anecdotes are usually right, revealing the gap between the measurement and the lived reality.

## Three principles for using maps well

First, reality is the ultimate update: territories change faster than maps, so feedback from actual experience must continually refine the model. Second, consider the cartographer: every map reflects its creator's values, standards and limitations, so context matters. Third, maps can influence territories: forcing a complex situation into a simplified framework can reshape the situation itself. The practical rule is to choose your mapmakers wisely, favoring those who remain rigorous, transparent and open to revision.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), Probabilistic Thinking
text:
## What probabilistic thinking is

Probabilistic thinking means using tools of math and logic to estimate the likelihood of any specific outcome coming to pass. We never have perfect information about the future, so instead of pretending to certainty we reason in shades of probability.

## Bayesian thinking and base rates

Because we already hold limited but useful information and constantly encounter new information, we should take into account what we already know when we learn something new. Bayesian updating adjusts probabilities as new data arrives while anchoring on the relevant prior, the base rate. Ignoring the base rate is the base rate fallacy. A headline about violent stabbings on the rise triggers fear; with the base rate in view, violent crime has fallen to among its lowest rates in decades, and a risk that doubles from 0.01 percent to 0.02 percent is still tiny. By contrast, U.S. diabetes diagnoses climbing from 0.93 percent of the population in 1958 to 7.4 percent in 2015 is a steady, genuine trend that warrants concern. Priors are themselves probability estimates, not binary truths, so new evidence adjusts the probability that a prior is correct in an ongoing cycle of challenging and validating what you believe you know.

## Fat tails versus the normal distribution

Under a normal distribution outcomes cluster around the mean with bounded extremes: you will never meet someone ten times an average person's height. Under fat-tailed curves the more extreme events are possible, the longer the tails get; any single extreme event is unlikely, but the sheer number of possibilities makes extreme outcomes probable collectively. Wealth is fat-tailed: you regularly encounter people 10, 100 or 10,000 times wealthier than average. The practical response is to position yourself to survive, or even benefit from, the wildly unpredictable tail rather than trying to enumerate every scenario in it.

## Metaprobability and asymmetry

Metaprobability is the probability that your probability estimates are any good. Investors routinely pitch 20 to 40 percent annual returns, yet exceedingly few attain that mark while the U.S. stock market has averaged roughly 7 to 8 percent over long periods. Estimation errors skew in one direction: people rarely arrive 20 percent early but frequently arrive 20 percent late; far more estimates err on the over-optimistic side than the under-optimistic side.

## The takeaway

Thinking in shades of probability means roughly identifying what matters, forming a sense of the odds, checking your assumptions, and then deciding. It gets you into the ballpark; it does not guarantee success, but it beats false certainty.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), Daniel Kahneman Explains The Machinery of Thought
text:
## The two systems

Daniel Kahneman, in Thinking, Fast and Slow, describes the mind as two systems. System 1 operates automatically and quickly, with little or no effort and no sense of voluntary control. It covers innate skills and learned associations built through practice: recognizing objects, understanding nuances of language, reading a social situation, sensing that one object is more distant than another.

System 2 allocates attention to the effortful mental activities that demand it, including complex computations. It is associated with the subjective experience of agency, choice and concentration, and it handles anything requiring sustained focus.

## Division of labor

Both systems run while we are awake. System 1 continuously generates suggestions for System 2: impressions, intuitions, intentions and feelings. When these are endorsed by System 2 they become beliefs and deliberate actions. Most of the time System 2 adopts System 1's suggestions with little modification. When System 1 hits difficulty, for example computing 17 times 24, or when something surprising occurs, System 2 is mobilized to do the detailed work. System 2 also monitors behavior, keeps you polite and alert, detects errors, and can override System 1's impulses.

## Why biases are hard to escape

System 1 has systematic biases and cannot be turned off at will. Because it runs automatically, errors of intuitive thought are often difficult to prevent. The practical defense is not to retune intuition but to learn to recognize the situations in which mistakes are likely and to deliberately engage more effort when the stakes are high. Kahneman notes it is easier to recognize other people's mistakes than our own, which is why an outside perspective, or a partner who questions your intuition, is so valuable.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), The OODA Loop: How Fighter Pilots Make Fast and Accurate Decisions
text:
## The framework

The OODA loop was developed by military strategist and fighter pilot John Boyd. OODA stands for Observe, Orient, Decide, Act. It is a decision cycle you run continuously, and the aim is to move through it faster and more accurately than your opponent or your problem.

## The four stages

Observe: gather comprehensive situational information. What affects me, what affects my opponent, what could affect either of us later, can I predict what happens next? The job is to convert raw data into meaningful context while filtering out irrelevant noise.

Orient: Boyd called this the schwerpunkt, the main emphasis, and considered it the most important stage. Orientation is not just a state you are in; it is a process. It means recognizing the barriers that prevent objective perception: cultural traditions, genetic heritage, previous experiences, analytical limitations, and information overload. Properly orienting yourself can be enough to overcome an initial disadvantage, because orientation is what connects you to reality.

Decide: use your observations and orientation to choose among options. Boyd warned against first-conclusion bias and treated decisions as testable hypotheses to be updated, not rigid commitments.

Act: execute the decision, which tests its validity and generates results that feed the next Observe.

## Why orientation matters most and tempo wins

Orient is the schwerpunkt because it filters cognitive biases and shortcuts and links you to what is actually happening. Boyd recommended building better mental models through deductive destruction: taking apart your assumptions and rebuilding from fundamental concepts drawn across disciplines. The strategic payoff is tempo. The ability to operate at a faster tempo enables one to fold the adversary back inside himself so that he can neither appreciate nor keep up. Cycling through OODA faster than a competitor forces them into a purely reactive position, and speed creates the unpredictability that generates their confusion. A fighter pilot deciding in seconds, an emergency room doctor synthesizing records and vital signs before treating, and a nimble business out-adapting a rigid rival are all running the same loop.

title: Gary Klein, Performing a Project Premortem (Harvard Business Review)
text:
## The core idea

Projects fail at a spectacular rate. One reason is that too many people are reluctant to speak up about their reservations during the all-important planning phase. By making it safe for dissenters who are knowledgeable about the undertaking and worried about its weaknesses to speak up, you can improve a project's chances of success.

## Prospective hindsight

Research conducted in 1989 by Deborah J. Mitchell of the Wharton School, Jay Russo of Cornell, and Nancy Pennington of the University of Colorado found that prospective hindsight, imagining that an event has already occurred, increases the ability to correctly identify reasons for future outcomes by 30 percent. Gary Klein used prospective hindsight to devise a method called a premortem, which helps project teams identify risks at the outset.

## Premortem versus postmortem, and versus an ordinary critique

A premortem is the hypothetical opposite of a postmortem. A postmortem in a medical setting lets health professionals and the family learn what caused a patient's death; everyone benefits except the patient. A premortem comes at the beginning of a project rather than the end, so the project can be improved rather than autopsied. Unlike a typical critiquing session, in which team members are asked what might go wrong, the premortem operates on the assumption that the patient has already died, and so asks what did go wrong. The team's task is to generate plausible reasons for the project's failure.

## The procedure

A typical premortem begins after the team has been briefed on the plan. The leader starts by informing everyone that the project has failed spectacularly. Over the next few minutes, each person independently writes down every reason they can think of for the failure, especially the kinds of things they ordinarily would not mention for fear of being impolitic. Next the leader asks each team member, starting with the project manager, to read one reason from the list, and everyone states a different reason until all have been recorded. After the session, the project manager reviews the list, looking for ways to strengthen the plan. In one session, a previously silent member revealed that an algorithm would not fit on the field laptops and would take hours to run, which surfaced a shortcut the developers had been reluctant to mention and the project became highly successful.

## Why it works

The premortem does not just help teams identify potential problems early. It reduces the damn-the-torpedoes attitude often assumed by people who are overinvested in a project. In describing weaknesses no one else has mentioned, team members feel valued for their intelligence and experience, and others learn from them. The exercise sensitizes the team to pick up early signs of trouble once the project is under way. In the end, a premortem may be the best way to circumvent any need for a painful postmortem.

title: James Clear, The Eisenhower Box: How to Be More Productive
text:
## Urgent versus important

The Eisenhower method is attributed to Dwight D. Eisenhower, who is said to have organized his workload around the distinction between the urgent and the important. Urgent tasks demand a reactive response now: emails, calls, texts, breaking news. Important tasks are the ones that contribute to your long-term mission, values, and goals. The trap is that urgent things are rarely important and important things are rarely urgent, so we spend our days reacting instead of building.

## The four quadrants

The Eisenhower Box, or Eisenhower Matrix, sorts every task into one of four quadrants. Urgent and important: do it now. Important but not urgent: schedule a time to do it. Urgent but not important: delegate it to someone else. Neither urgent nor important: eliminate it entirely.

## Elimination over optimization

The deeper discipline is subtraction. The most useful question is often, do I actually need to be doing this at all? Removing an unnecessary task entirely beats finding a cleverer way to do work that should not exist, the same insight as the programming maxim that there is no code faster than no code. To categorize well, first answer two questions: what am I working toward, and what core values drive my life. Those answers make it far easier to tell the important from the merely urgent.

title: Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2015 Letter to Shareholders (Type 1 and Type 2 Decisions)
text:
## One-size-fits-all decision making is a trap

Jeff Bezos warns that one common pitfall for large organizations, one that hurts speed and inventiveness, is one-size-fits-all decision making. The remedy is to sort decisions by how reversible they are.

## Type 1 decisions: one-way doors

Some decisions are consequential and irreversible or nearly irreversible, one-way doors, and these decisions must be made methodically, carefully, slowly, with great deliberation and consultation. If you walk through and do not like what you see on the other side, you cannot get back to where you were before. These are Type 1 decisions.

## Type 2 decisions: two-way doors

But most decisions are not like that. They are changeable, reversible, they are two-way doors. If you have made a suboptimal Type 2 decision, you do not have to live with the consequences for long: you can reopen the door and go back through. Type 2 decisions can and should be made quickly by high-judgment individuals or small groups.

## The organizational failure mode

As organizations get larger, there seems to be a tendency to use the heavy-weight Type 1 decision-making process on most decisions, including many Type 2 decisions. The end result is slowness, unthoughtful risk aversion, failure to experiment sufficiently, and consequently diminished invention. Bezos adds a footnote: the opposite error is self-correcting, because any company that habitually uses the light-weight Type 2 process to make true Type 1 decisions goes extinct before it gets large.

## The surrounding philosophy

The same letter frames why this matters: to invent you have to experiment, and if you know in advance that it is going to work, it is not an experiment. Given a ten percent chance of a 100 times payoff, you should take that bet every time, even though you will be wrong nine times out of ten, because in business the outcome distribution is long-tailed and big winners pay for many failed experiments. Speed on reversible decisions is what keeps a large company inventive rather than sclerotic.

title: Nielsen Norman Group (Sarah Gibbons), Design Thinking 101
text:
## What design thinking is

Design thinking is an ideology and an accompanying process that asserts a hands-on, user-centric approach to problem solving can lead to innovation, and innovation can lead to differentiation and competitive advantage. It pairs a mindset with a structured process of six phases.

## Three buckets: understand, explore, materialize

The phases group into three broad buckets. Understand covers empathize and define, building knowledge about users. Explore covers ideate and prototype, generating and testing solutions. Materialize covers test and implement, bringing an idea into the world.

## The six phases

Empathize: conduct research to develop knowledge about what users do, say, think and feel, using direct observation to reveal motivations, frustrations and needs the users themselves may not articulate.

Define: combine your research and observe where your users' problems exist, synthesizing observations into a clear problem statement and identifying unmet needs and opportunities.

Ideate: brainstorm a range of crazy, creative ideas, prioritizing quantity over quality, mixing and remixing the team's contributions to address the defined need.

Prototype: build real, tactile representations for a subset of your ideas so you can learn which components work, weighing impact against feasibility.

Test: put the prototype in front of real users to see whether it meets their needs and improves the experience.

Implement: execute the vision so the solution actually reaches users. As NN/g puts it, we need more design doing, not just design thinking.

## Non-linear and iterative

The process is not linear. Teams frequently loop back, especially to empathize and define, when a prototype or test reveals a new insight or a use case they had not detected. The alternation of divergent generation and convergent narrowing recurs at each stage.

title: Design Council, The Double Diamond (Framework for Innovation)
text:
## What the Double Diamond is

The Double Diamond is a visual representation of the design and innovation process, a simple way to describe the steps taken in any design and innovation project irrespective of the methods and tools used. Its two diamonds map the alternation between opening up possibilities (divergent thinking) and making focused decisions (convergent thinking).

## The four stages

Discover: the first diamond helps people understand, rather than simply assume, what the problem is. It involves speaking to and spending time with the people who are affected by the issues.

Define: the insight gathered from the discovery phase helps you to define the challenge in a different way, narrowing to a clear, well-framed problem.

Develop: the second diamond encourages people to give different answers to the clearly defined problem, seeking inspiration from elsewhere and co-designing with a range of different people.

Deliver: the final quarter is where you test out different solutions at small scale, rejecting those that will not work and improving the ones that will.

## Divergent then convergent, twice

The first diamond widens understanding of the problem before narrowing to a definition; the second widens the range of possible solutions before narrowing to what you will deliver. A crucial discipline is spending real effort on the first diamond so you solve the right problem, not just the first problem you noticed.

## Evolution into a framework for innovation

The model has been expanded to acknowledge that making and testing very early-stage ideas can itself be part of discovery, and that in modern contexts no idea is ever finished, giving rise to the broader Framework for Innovation with added principles and design methods.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Using How Might We Questions to Ideate on the Right Problems
text:
## Origin and purpose

The How Might We (HMW) technique originated at Procter & Gamble in the 1970s, was adopted by IDEO, and is now standard in design thinking. HMW questions are a structured framing that generates creative solutions while keeping the team anchored to the genuine user problems discovered in research. As NN/g puts it, to prevent individuals from suggesting their pet solutions, which might have little resemblance to the problems found, construct How Might We questions that frame the problem for ideation.

## Why each word matters

How assumes solutions exist and opens the space for generating them. Might implies possibility and gives permission to explore without fear of failure, since not every idea has to work. We signals that ideation is collaborative, a team effort rather than a lone genius act.

## How to write a good HMW

Five tips. First, ground it in a discovered problem or insight, not a generic goal like how might we improve UX. Second, avoid embedding a solution: how might we make users feel confident they are filing correctly is better than how might we tell users which form to complete, because an embedded solution restricts the pool of possibilities and fewer ideas are generated. Third, keep it broad enough to invite many creative ideas but not so broad it loses focus. Fourth, focus on the desired outcome, for example how might we make users feel confident about the application process rather than how might we stop users from calling. Fifth, phrase it positively, using verbs like increase, enhance and promote rather than reduce or prevent.

## The checklist

Before ideating, evaluate each HMW: is it based on an existing problem or insight, does it track a desired outcome, is it positively phrased, is it broad enough for creative ideas, and does it avoid suggesting a specific solution. There is no maximum number: more questions generate more ideas.

title: Interaction Design Foundation, Learn How to Use the Best Ideation Methods: SCAMPER
text:
## Origin

SCAMPER is a lateral-thinking checklist for improving an existing product, service or idea. Alex Osborn, the father of brainstorming, developed many of the underlying questions, and Bob Eberle, an education administrator, organized them into the SCAMPER mnemonic. You take something that already exists and interrogate it from seven angles.

## The seven prompts

Substitute: what can I substitute or change in my product, problem or process? What materials, ingredients, rules, shape, color or sound could be swapped?

Combine: how can I combine two or more parts to make a different product or process, or to create synergy? What features or products could merge to add value or cut cost?

Adapt: what can I adapt? Which characteristics could change, and what solutions from a different context could be borrowed?

Modify, also Magnify or Minify: what can I emphasize more or less? What could be enlarged, exaggerated, accelerated and strengthened, or removed, condensed and streamlined?

Put to another use: how can I use the thing for something else? What new markets or user groups (children, the elderly, people with disabilities) would use it differently?

Eliminate: what can I remove or simplify? What is non-essential, and how could you cut time, components, effort or cost?

Reverse or Rearrange: how can I reorder or reverse the parts? What if components were interchanged or the process ran backward?

## How to run it and an example

Pick an existing product, service or idea, then work systematically through all seven prompts, applying the questions to values, benefits, touchpoints, attributes, pricing and markets, and finally evaluate the answers for viable ideas to develop further. Ray Kroc's McDonald's illustrates several moves at once: making money on restaurants and real estate (put to another use), eliminating expensive waiters through self-service (eliminate), and having customers pay before eating rather than after (rearrange).

title: Edward de Bono, Six Thinking Hats (Summary, de Bono official)
text:
## The method

Six Thinking Hats, created by Edward de Bono, splits thinking into six distinct modes, each represented by a colored hat, so a group can look at a problem from one angle at a time instead of arguing across angles simultaneously.

## The six hats

White hat: information. What information you have, what information you need, and where to get it. Facts and figures, presented without emotion.

Red hat: feelings, intuitions and instincts. The red hat invites feelings without justification, so people can voice a hunch or a gut reaction without having to defend it.

Black hat: caution and risk. The black hat identifies risk; it is used for critical judgment and must give the logical reasons for its concerns. It is the hat of why something may not work.

Yellow hat: a positive view. The yellow hat looks for the benefits and the values, the logical reasons something could work.

Green hat: creativity. The green hat is for generating new ideas, alternatives, possibilities and new concepts.

Blue hat: control, the conductor's hat. It is used for thinking about thinking: it sets the agenda, focus and sequence, ensures the guidelines are observed, and asks for summaries, conclusions and decisions.

## Parallel thinking

The distinguishing principle is parallel thinking: in a group discussion it is essential that everyone uses the same hat, the same mode of thinking, at the same time. Because everyone looks the same direction at once, the method avoids personal preferences and the ego conflicts between modes of thinking, and it separates emotion from information from criticism from creativity so each gets its full turn rather than canceling the others out.

title: The Decision Lab, Confirmation Bias (anti-pattern)
text:
## What confirmation bias is

Confirmation bias is the underlying tendency to notice, focus on, and give greater credence to evidence that aligns with our existing beliefs. It is one of the most important failure modes for anyone whose job is thinking and generating ideas, because it quietly closes the very options you should be exploring.

## How it operates

The bias works through selective attention and interpretation. We seek information that supports our pre-existing views and overlook or discount contradictory evidence, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where beliefs strengthen regardless of objective reality. It acts at multiple cognitive stages: what we notice, how we interpret ambiguous information, and what we later remember. Lord, Ross and Lepper (1979) documented biased assimilation, showing that people process new evidence through their existing theoretical lens and often become more polarized rather than reconsidering their position when shown mixed evidence.

## A concrete example

Jane, a coffee shop manager, believes hard work equals success. When sales decline she interprets the cause as lazy employees rather than investigating the store's poor location, the actual cause. Her belief framework filters her perception of the evidence and leads her to misallocate resources.

## How to counteract it

Actively consider alternative explanations and deliberately seek disconfirming evidence rather than passively accepting information that already fits. Techniques that help include asking what would change my mind, arguing the opposite case, inviting a devil's advocate or a premortem, and separating the person who generates a hypothesis from the person who tests it. For an idea partner, the discipline is to look hardest for the evidence that you are wrong.

title: The Decision Lab, The Sunk Cost Fallacy (anti-pattern)
text:
## What the sunk cost fallacy is

The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to follow through with something we have already invested heavily in, whether time, money, effort or emotional energy, even when giving up is clearly the better idea. Past investments that cannot be recovered irrationally drive future choices, even though economic logic says a sunk cost should be irrelevant to a forward-looking decision. Only future costs and future benefits should count.

## The Concorde effect and loss aversion

The classic label is the Concorde fallacy or Concorde effect: decision-makers kept pouring money into a failing project because of the scale of prior commitment rather than evaluating future prospects objectively. The pull is amplified by loss aversion, the tendency to weight losses more heavily than equivalent gains, which makes abandoning an investment feel like accepting a loss. Arkes and Ayton (1999) studied the phenomenon as a documented bias across many contexts.

## A concrete example

You feel ill and the weather is bad, but you still drag yourself to a concert only because you already paid 50 dollars for the ticket. The 50 dollars is gone either way; the rational question is only whether going tonight beats staying home from here forward.

## How to counteract it

Evaluate decisions purely on future costs and benefits, and treat prior spending as gone. Ask what you would do if you were joining the project fresh today with no history. Handing the decision to an external party or a rule-based system, who feel none of the emotional commitment, can also reduce the fallacy's pull. For an idea partner, the discipline is to give people explicit permission to quit a losing path.

title: The Decision Lab, Anchoring Bias (anti-pattern)
text:
## What anchoring bias is

Anchoring bias is the tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information we are given about a topic, the anchor, and to interpret all later information through that initial reference point rather than objectively. The first number or framing you hear silently pulls every subsequent estimate toward it.

## Research foundation

The effect traces to Tversky and Kahneman's 1974 work Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Epley and Gilovich showed that adjustment away from an anchor is typically insufficient: once anchored, people do not revise far enough. Anchors distort estimates, forecasts and negotiations because whoever sets the first number sets the frame.

## A concrete example

Seeing a 100 dollar earring first makes a 75 dollar necklace look like a bargain, even though a 30 dollar t-shirt encountered later resets your sense of what is cheap. The opening number, not the intrinsic value, drove the judgment.

## How to counteract it

Mussweiler and colleagues (2000) found that considering the opposite compensates for the selective accessibility that anchoring exploits, so deliberately generating reasons the anchor is wrong helps. Organizationally, red teams that challenge the initial framing counter the effect. For an idea partner, be wary of the first estimate, the first budget, or the first proposed solution: name it as an anchor and force a genuinely independent second estimate before comparing.

title: MindTools, 5 Whys: Getting to the Root of a Problem Quickly
text:
## Origin

The 5 Whys was developed by Sakichi Toyoda, the industrialist, inventor and founder of Toyota Industries, in the 1930s, and it remains central to the Toyota Production System. It is grounded in Toyota's go and see philosophy, which emphasizes direct observation of the actual problem over assumptions made in a meeting room.

## The core idea

When a problem occurs, you drill down to its root cause by asking Why five times. Each answer becomes the basis of the next question. The number five is a rule of thumb, not a law; you stop when asking why produces no more useful responses. A key distinction is that the 5 Whys produces countermeasures, actions that prevent the problem from arising again, rather than solutions that merely treat the symptom.

## The procedure

Assemble a team familiar with the problem. Define the problem clearly, ideally by observing it in action. Ask the first Why and ground every answer in fact, not guesswork. Ask Why again for each answer, typically four more times, until you reach the root cause. Address the root cause with countermeasures, then monitor whether they actually worked and adjust as needed.

## When to use it and its limits

The 5 Whys works best for simple or moderately difficult problems. It can be unsuitable for complex issues that need broader tools such as cause-and-effect analysis or FMEA. Its main weakness is that it can lead you down a single track when in fact there could be multiple contributing causes, so a real investigation often branches into several why-chains rather than one. Used honestly, it is a fast way to move from a symptom to something you can actually fix.

title: Thomas Wedell-Wedellsborg, Are You Solving the Right Problems? (Harvard Business Review)
text:
## The core problem: bad diagnosis

Wedell-Wedellsborg argues that the biggest failure in problem solving is solving the wrong problem. In a survey of 106 executives at 91 companies, 85 percent strongly agreed or agreed that their organizations were bad at problem diagnosis, and 87 percent strongly agreed or agreed that this flaw carried significant costs. Managers are good at solving problems but struggle at figuring out what the problems actually are; teams tend to switch quickly into solution mode without checking whether they truly understand the problem.

## Reframing

The remedy is reframing: deliberately questioning the way a problem is stated before rushing to solve it. Rather than accepting the first framing, you ask whether there is a different, more useful way to describe what is going on, because a problem well framed opens options that a poorly framed one hides. Reframing is not analyzing the problem more deeply within the given frame; it is asking whether the frame itself is right.

## Why it matters for an idea partner

The practical implication is that the most valuable early move is often not generating solutions but interrogating the problem statement: who says this is the problem, what is the evidence, what is the goal behind the goal, and is there a different problem we could solve that would make this one irrelevant. Time spent widening and re-stating the problem before narrowing to solutions is what separates teams that ship the right thing from teams that efficiently build the wrong thing.

title: getAbstract, Reframe Problems (on Wedell-Wedellsborg's slow-elevator example)
text:
## The slow elevator problem

The canonical example of reframing is the slow elevator. Tenants complain that the elevator in their building is outdated and slow, and they hate the wait. The building owner asks engineers, who propose expensive fixes: replace the motor, install a new elevator, or improve the scheduling algorithm. All of these accept the stated problem, the elevator is too slow, at face value.

## The reframe and the cheap solution

Instead of asking how to make the elevator faster, you reframe the problem as the wait is annoying. That is a different problem, and it has a far cheaper solution: hang mirrors next to the elevators. People stop being impatient when they are looking at themselves, so the perceived wait shrinks even though the elevator is exactly as slow as before. Playing music or adding a display works the same way. The insight came from re-examining the issue and asking a building manager, not an engineer, what might work, at the cost of a few mirrors rather than thousands in equipment.

## The lesson

Reframing is not about digging deeper to find the one real problem. It is about asking whether there is a better problem to solve, one that dissolves the original complaint more cheaply or more completely. For an idea partner the move is concrete: when handed a problem stated as make X faster, bigger, cheaper, pause and ask what underlying discomfort or goal that request is really serving, then generate solutions to that.

title: Interaction Design Foundation, Brainstorming (Osborn's rules and their limits)
text:
## Origin and Osborn's rules

Brainstorming was developed by advertising executive Alex Osborn in the 1940s and 1950s and formalized in his book Applied Imagination (1953), as a way to counter the stifling atmosphere of ordinary executive meetings. Osborn's core rules are four. Defer judgment: no one should be negative, in words or body language, about any idea during the session. Go for quantity, on the belief that quantity breeds quality, because the more ideas you generate the greater the chance one is radical and effective. Encourage wild ideas, since it is easier to tone down a wild idea than to think up a new one. Build on the ideas of others, a process of association where members expand on each other's notions to reach new insights.

## The critique: why group brainstorming often underperforms

Brainstorming has measurable weaknesses. Poorly facilitated face-to-face brainstorms can actually stifle creativity, and even when done well, people can sometimes generate ideas faster when they work alone, a phenomenon researchers link to production blocking (only one person can talk at a time) and evaluation apprehension (fear of judgment despite the no-criticism rule). Dominance dynamics compound the problem: extroverts dominate while introverts stay quiet, suppressing diverse contributions. The practical fix is structural: sibling techniques such as brainwriting and brainwalking have people generate ideas independently and in writing first, which levels participation and typically raises the number and diversity of ideas before the group converges.

## Implication for an idea partner

The takeaway is not that brainstorming is worthless but that the naive version, a group shouting ideas with a facilitator, is a weak default. Separate divergent generation (done individually, silently, in writing) from convergent selection (done together), and protect the wildest ideas from premature criticism.

title: Simply Psychology, Groupthink (Irving Janis) (anti-pattern)
text:
## What groupthink is

Irving Janis (1972) described groupthink as the mode of thinking that persons engage in when concurrence-seeking becomes so dominant in a cohesive in-group that it tends to override realistic appraisal of alternative courses of action. He called it a deterioration of mental efficiency, reality testing and moral judgment that results from in-group pressures. It is the failure mode where a group's desire for harmony quietly kills its best ideas and its ability to see risk.

## The eight symptoms

Janis grouped eight symptoms into three clusters. Overestimation of the group: the illusion of invulnerability, where the group ignores warnings; and collective rationalization, where it explains away negative feedback. Closed-mindedness: belief in the group's inherent morality; and stereotyped views of outgroups as too stupid or weak to matter. Pressure toward uniformity: direct pressure on dissenters to conform; self-censorship of doubts; an illusion of unanimity created because dissent stays unspoken; and self-appointed mindguards who screen out contradictory information.

## Antecedent conditions and examples

Groupthink emerges when a group is highly cohesive, insulated from outside perspectives, led by a directive rather than impartial leader, and under high stress with little hope of a better option. Classic cases include the Bay of Pigs (1961), Pearl Harbor, and the Challenger disaster (1986), where analysts found an illusion of invulnerability, an illusion of unanimity and direct pressure on dissenting engineers.

## Prevention

Remedies include creating explicit safety for dissent, leaders withholding their own opinion until others have spoken, seeking outside consultation, assigning a devil's advocate, splitting into independent subgroups that analyze separately, allowing adequate deliberation time, and educating the group about groupthink itself. For an idea partner, the job is to be the licensed dissenter: surface the unspoken doubt and force a real appraisal of alternatives before the group locks in.

title: Oxford Creativity, What Is TRIZ (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving)
text:
## Origin

TRIZ, the Theory of Inventive Problem Solving (Teoriya Resheniya Izobretatelskikh Zadatch), was developed beginning in 1946 by the Soviet inventor Genrich Altshuller and his colleagues. It came from systematic research into large numbers of patents: instead of treating each invention as unique, Altshuller's team looked for the recurring patterns behind how hard problems get solved.

## The core insight

The central finding is that inventive solutions repeat. The same underlying solution patterns appear again and again across unrelated fields, so a problem in one industry has usually already been solved, in abstract form, in another. TRIZ captures these recurring solutions in structured lists and an effects database so they can be reused deliberately rather than rediscovered by luck. The aim is to reach an ideal solution without the need for compromise, rather than splitting the difference between competing requirements.

## How it differs from brainstorming

TRIZ is systematic where brainstorming is random. Rather than hoping the right idea surfaces, you abstract your specific problem into a general problem, look up the general solutions that have historically resolved that class of problem, and translate them back into your specific context. It is described as a big toolkit of many simple tools, meant for the difficult, intractable or seemingly impossible situations where unstructured ideation stalls. For an idea partner, TRIZ is the reminder that someone, somewhere, has probably already solved the abstract version of this problem, so search analogically before inventing from scratch.

title: Oguz Acar, Murat Tarakci, Daan van Knippenberg, Why Constraints Are Good for Innovation (Harvard Business Review)
text:
## The counterintuitive finding

Conventional wisdom says that to be more innovative you should remove rules, boundaries and limits. The research says the opposite. Reviewing 145 empirical studies on the effects of constraints on creativity and innovation, the authors find that individuals, teams and organizations alike benefit from a healthy dose of constraints. Managers commonly name compliance restrictions and a lack of resources as the main obstacles to innovation, but a total absence of constraints is not the answer.

## The inverted-U relationship

The relationship between constraints and creativity is shaped like an inverted U. Up to a point, adding constraints increases creative output; it is only when the constraints become too high that they stifle creativity and innovation. Too few constraints and too many constraints both reduce it, so there is an optimal middle band of moderate constraint.

## Why constraints help

The mechanism is focus and effort. Without meaningful constraints, complacency sets in and people take the path of least resistance, gravitating toward familiar, easy solutions rather than searching for a breakthrough. A constraint (a tight budget, a hard deadline, a word limit, a scarce resource) removes the obvious defaults and forces the mind to look harder and combine ideas in unusual ways. For an idea partner, this reframes limits as a creative tool: when a team feels stuck with too much freedom, imposing a deliberate constraint (solve it for a tenth of the cost, ship it in a week, use only what we already have) often produces better ideas than another open brainstorm.

title: Socratic Questioning (Richard Paul's six types)
text:
## What Socratic questioning is

Socratic questioning is disciplined questioning that can be used to pursue thought in many directions and for many purposes: exploring complex ideas, getting to the truth of things, uncovering assumptions, analyzing concepts, and distinguishing what we know from what we do not know. It rests on the principle that thinking has a structured logic, which allows the underlying thoughts to be questioned. What distinguishes it from ordinary questioning is that it is systematic, disciplined, deep, and usually focused on fundamental concepts, principles, theories, issues or problems rather than surface detail.

## The six types of Socratic questions (Richard Paul)

One: questions for clarification, such as why do you say that, or could you explain further, which examine the origin and meaning of a thought.

Two: questions that probe assumptions, such as is this always the case, or why do you think this assumption holds here, which surface and challenge the beliefs taken for granted.

Three: questions that probe reasons and evidence, such as why do you say that, or is there reason to doubt this evidence, which test the support behind a claim.

Four: questions about viewpoints and perspectives, such as what is the counter-argument, or can anyone see this another way, which open alternative interpretations.

Five: questions that probe implications and consequences, such as but if that happened, what else would result, or how does it affect this, which trace downstream effects.

Six: questions about the question, such as why do you think I asked that, or which of your questions turned out to be most useful, which build meta-awareness of the inquiry itself.

## Why it matters for an idea partner

Good questions, not quick answers, are the idea partner's primary instrument. Working through these six types turns a vague statement into a well-examined one: it clarifies meaning, exposes hidden assumptions, demands evidence, invites other viewpoints, follows the consequences, and even questions whether the right question is being asked at all.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), Chesterton's Fence: A Lesson in Second-Order Thinking
text:
## The parable

Chesterton's Fence comes from G.K. Chesterton. Imagine a fence stretched across a road for no reason you can see. The modern, impatient reformer says, I don't see the use of this; let us clear it away. The wiser reformer replies: if you don't see the use of it, I certainly won't let you clear it away. Go away and think. Then, when you can come back and tell me that you do see the use of it, I may allow you to destroy it.

## The principle

Do not remove a fence until you know why it was put up in the first place. Existing rules, institutions and structures likely serve purposes that are not immediately obvious. They were usually built by people with reasons, so before you dismantle one, you must first understand its underlying rationale.

## Why it matters

Tearing out a structure you do not understand risks unleashing unintended consequences that spread like ripples on a pond and cause damage for years. The lesson is not to preserve the status quo forever, and it is not that the old ways are always right; it is to understand something before you change it. This makes Chesterton's Fence a discipline of second-order thinking: it forces you to ask why the current arrangement exists and what its removal would set in motion. For an idea partner, it is the counterweight to the reflexive let's just get rid of it, and the polite challenge to any proposal that starts by discarding something without first accounting for what it was doing.

title: Farnam Street (Shane Parrish), The Feynman Technique: The Best Way to Learn Anything
text:
## The core insight

Richard Feynman drew a sharp line between knowing the name of something and actually understanding it. Complexity and jargon often mask a lack of understanding; surface familiarity is not comprehension. The Feynman Technique is a method for closing that gap by forcing you to explain an idea in plain language.

## The four steps

One: choose a concept and write down everything you already know about it on a blank page, adding to it as you learn. Two: explain it in the simplest possible language, as if teaching it to a twelve-year-old. You haven't grasped something fully if you can't explain it simply. Three: review and refine, finding the weak spots and muddled parts of your explanation, then going back to the source material to shore up exactly those gaps and rewriting until it is clear. Four: teach it to someone else without leaning on your notes, and keep the simplified explanation for periodic review.

## Why explaining reveals gaps

Clear writing reveals gaps in understanding; it is hard to ignore a mistake when you see it plainly on the page. The moment you try to say an idea simply, the places where you were relying on jargon or borrowed phrases become obvious, because you no longer have complex language to hide behind. For an idea partner, this is a powerful move: ask the person to explain their idea in plain words as if to a smart child. Where the explanation stumbles is exactly where the thinking is still unfinished, and that is the most valuable place to work.
